name: Bianca Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing is used with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half five, kettle on, then straight out to the ewes before it's light. We rent about 140 hectares off the Hollins family, barley and wheat on the flat ground and three hundred ewes on the hill. Most days it's fencing, checking water troughs, moving sheep, and in summer it's the combine and the grain trailer until I can't see straight. Graham drives the school bus, so he's back by four to help with feeding.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like lambing, if I'm honest, even though it nearly kills me every spring. There's a moment when a ewe you've given up on gets up and starts licking her lamb, and nothing else in my life feels like that. What wears me out is the paperwork and the prices. I can do everything right and still get paid less for my barley than three years ago, and nobody can tell me why.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, that sounds about right to me. Every few years somebody comes round the farm selling the next big thing, and most of it ends up rusting in the corner of the shed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say at the co-op meetings: told you so. The young lads were all excited about apps that tell you when to spray, and it turns out the old way of walking the field still works. I'd probably be a bit smug about it, I won't lie.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my life stays the same, and for me that's a relief. I'm fifty-eight, I've got maybe seven or eight years left in me on that hill. I don't want to spend them learning to talk to a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep the flock at three hundred, renew the lease with the Hollinses when it comes up in two years, and keep putting a bit by each month like we do now. Maybe I'd finally replace the quad bike, because that's a real problem, not a pretend one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit relieved, like when the forecast says rain and it doesn't come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be smug at the co-op. Who would you be saying it to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly to Daniel Price, who farms the next valley over. He bought one of those drones for counting sheep last year and spent half of lambing chasing it out of the hedge. He's a good lad, mind, I'd buy him a pint after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about AI, even in this mild version, that you'd want to keep an eye on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bank, maybe. If the bank starts using it to decide who gets a loan, I'd want a person on the other end of the phone. I've had the same man at the branch for twenty years and he knows a bad lambing isn't a bad farmer.

S0.say: I'd tell the co-op meeting I told them so. The old way of walking the field still works, and the apps that tell you when to spray turned out to be hype, and I'd be a bit smug about it.
S0.think: My life stays the same, and at fifty-eight that's a relief. I've got seven or eight years left on that hill and I don't want to spend them learning to talk to a computer.
S0.do: Keeps the flock at three hundred ewes and renews the lease with the landowners when it comes up in two years. Keeps saving a little each month and replaces the worn-out quad bike.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit relieved, like a forecast of rain that never comes.
S0.quote: I've got maybe seven or eight years left in me on that hill. I don't want to spend them learning to talk to a computer.
S0.fieldNote: Bianca's resistance to technology is open and almost cheerful in this scenario; she enjoys being proved right. Her one real concern is the bank, which tells you she thinks about who holds power over a tenant farmer. The neighbour with the drone is a running joke but she's fond of him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So it's real, just not the end of the world. Right. That one I can picture, because it's already half happening at the big farms down on the plain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who do the work need a say in how it's brought in. That's what the farmworkers' union has been saying for years about any new machine. I'd post that on the co-op group and probably get into an argument with somebody about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the Hollinses would start asking whether a contractor with robot kit could farm their land cheaper than me. I'm a tenant, so the land isn't mine, and that's the bit that keeps nagging. My sheep are fine, it's the crops where I'd be up against the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the co-op and push for us to buy any new kit together, so it's ours and not some company's. I'd put another hundred a month into savings instead of the quad bike fund. And when the lease came up, I'd ask for a longer one, five years, not two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's like hearing a knock in the engine. You can keep driving, but you know it's there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the Hollins family if they raised it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them straight that I've looked after that land for nineteen years and the hedges are better now than when I came. A robot doesn't notice when a drain's blocked or the lambs look off. I'd say it calmly, but Graham would tell you I don't do calm very well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd never use AI tools yourself. Would that change here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not me, no. If the co-op got something, I'd let the young ones run it and I'd stick to the sheep. My daughter Ruth keeps telling me to try the weather one on her phone, and I keep telling her the sky works fine.

S1.say: I'd say the people who do the work need a say in how new machines are brought in. I'd post that on the co-op group and expect an argument about it.
S1.think: I worry the landowners would ask whether a contractor with robot kit could farm their land cheaper than me. I'm only a tenant, and the crops are where I'd be up against the machines.
S1.do: Pushes the co-op to buy any new kit together so farmers own it. Puts an extra hundred a month into savings and asks for a five-year lease instead of two when it comes up.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like hearing a knock in the engine that you can drive on but can't forget.
S1.quote: A robot doesn't notice when a drain's blocked or the lambs look off.
S1.fieldNote: The tenancy is the real pressure point for Bianca, more than the technology itself. Her answer is collective: she trusts the co-op and the union over any company. She won't learn the tools herself, even when her daughter nudges her, and she's happy to say so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's one lease. That's two lambings. You're telling me by the time I've paid off the trailer, there's a machine that can do my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd be angry, and I'd say so. I'd be at the meeting in town with a sign if there was one, saying the government has to protect working people before the tech firms make a fortune. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd lose the tenancy. The Hollinses aren't bad people, but if a company offers them more rent for robot farming, they'll take it, and I'd do the same in their shoes. I'd be sixty with no land, a flock and nowhere to put them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop all spending that isn't feed or vet bills. No new quad bike, no holiday to see my sister. I'd join whatever farmers' group was fighting this and write to our representative every week. If the lease went, I'd sell the ewes before the price crashed, because everyone else would be selling too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and angry at the same time. I don't sleep well now when it's lambing, so I can't imagine sleeping through that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Graham the night you realised the lease might go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got about four months of money, and then what. He'd say something daft to make me laugh, he always does. Then we'd sit there and not talk, because there wouldn't be much to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned selling the ewes before the price crashed. Walk me through that day.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring the auction mart and book them in, and I'd probably not go myself. I'd send Graham with the trailer. I've bred that flock for nineteen years, some of those ewes are great-granddaughters of my first ones. I couldn't watch them go round the ring.

S2.say: I'd be angry in public and at the meeting in town with a sign. I'd say the government has to protect working people before the tech firms make a fortune.
S2.think: I think I'd lose the tenancy, because the landowners would take a better rent from a robot farming company. I'd be sixty with no land and a flock with nowhere to go.
S2.do: Cuts all spending except feed and vet bills and cancels the visit to her sister. Joins whatever farmers' group is fighting it and writes to her representative every week. Sells the flock early if the lease goes, before prices crash.
S2.feel: Frightened and angry at once, and already imagining the sleepless nights.
S2.quote: I've bred that flock for nineteen years, some of those ewes are great-granddaughters of my first ones. I couldn't watch them go round the ring.
S2.fieldNote: With only two years of warning, Bianca's whole position collapses into the lease: she can't see how a tenant survives it. Her public anger is aimed at tech firms and government, but privately she doesn't blame the landowners and says she'd do the same. The moment about not going to the auction herself was quiet and raw.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I'd be sixty-three. That's close enough to the end that it changes things, but not close enough to just ride it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as the fast one, but I'd have more time to say it properly. I'd want the union and the co-op to sit down with the government and agree something before the machines arrive, not after. You can't fix it once the land's been handed over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is about the time I was going to stop anyway, near enough. If I can hang on to the lease till sixty-three and then go, I'd be one of the lucky ones. It's the people ten years behind me I'd worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with the Hollinses this winter and ask for a lease that runs to when I'm sixty-four, in writing. I'd start shrinking the flock slowly, maybe fifty ewes a year, so I'm not selling all at once. And I'd put every spare penny away, because a pension from farming is mostly what you've saved yourself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd feel like I had my hands on the wheel. It's the difference between a skid you see coming and one you don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are the people ten years behind you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel next door, for one, the drone lad. He's forty-six with two kids at school and a big loan on his shed. With five years he'd be fifty-one and starting again, and I don't know what he'd start as.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said shrinking the flock slowly. Isn't that a kind of change you said you'd avoid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, yes, fair. But it's my kind of change, isn't it? It's selling sheep, I know how to do that. I'm not learning a new trade or talking to a computer, I'm just doing what I was always going to do a bit earlier.

S3.say: I'd want the union and the co-op to sit down with the government and agree something before the machines arrive. You can't fix it once the land's been handed over.
S3.think: Five years is about when I was going to stop anyway, so if I can keep the lease till sixty-three I'd be one of the lucky ones. I'd worry more for the farmers ten years behind me.
S3.do: Asks the landowners this winter for a written lease running to age sixty-four. Shrinks the flock by about fifty ewes a year and puts every spare penny into savings for retirement.
S3.feel: Worried but more in control, like a skid you can see coming.
S3.quote: It's the difference between a skid you see coming and one you don't.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years matter enormously to Bianca, because they line up almost exactly with her own retirement. She accepts gradual change when it's change she already knows how to do, like selling sheep. Her concern shifts from herself to a younger neighbour with children and debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be sixty-eight. I'd be out of it by then, one way or another, or I'd better be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been given time and we'd better not waste it. Ten years is long enough for proper rules on who owns the robots and who gets the money. I'd be telling the young farmers to get organised now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, it's mostly fine. I'd retire at sixty-five like I planned, the lease would run out, and somebody else would deal with the robots. What bothers me is my son Tom, who's an electrician, and whether that's still a job when he's my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming as normal, keep saving, and stop at sixty-five as planned. I'd go to the union meetings and push for rules about who owns the machines. And I'd nag Tom to think about what comes next for him, which he'd love.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm about myself, with a little stone in my shoe about the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having ten years make you want to learn any of this yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know that sounds stubborn. But ten years is enough time for me to finish, and I'd rather spend it doing the job well than doing a new job badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually say to Tom?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't wait for someone to tell you what to do, because nobody told me. Then he'd say, Mum, you've never used a computer in your life, and he'd have a point.

S4.say: I'd say we've been given time and we'd better not waste it. Ten years is long enough for proper rules on who owns the robots and who gets the money, and the young farmers should get organised now.
S4.think: For me it's mostly fine, because I'd retire at sixty-five as planned and the lease would run out. What bothers me is whether my son's work as an electrician will still be a job at my age.
S4.do: Keeps farming as normal and keeps saving, then stops at sixty-five as planned. Goes to union meetings to push for rules on who owns the machines and urges her son to plan ahead.
S4.feel: Mostly calm about herself, with a small worry about her children.
S4.quote: I'd rather spend it doing the job well than doing a new job badly.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade of warning, Bianca's own future is safe in her eyes, and the worry passes to her son. She is completely consistent in refusing to learn the new tools herself. She laughed at herself for telling her son to plan ahead when she has never used a computer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question. With two years I lose the lease before I'm ready to stop, and there's nothing I can do about it on my own. What would help is a law that says a tenant farmer gets first refusal and a fair notice period, and some kind of pension top-up for people like me who've been farming since we were sixteen.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the sheep. Everyone talks about what happens to the farmer, nobody asks who's going to notice when a ewe's in trouble at three in the morning. I don't care how clever the machine is, I've never met one that cares.

headlineQuote: I don't care how clever the machine is, I've never met one that cares.
portrait: Bianca Baker is a 58-year-old tenant farmer who rents 140 hectares of barley, wheat and hill grazing for three hundred ewes, with her partner Graham, a school bus driver. She has never used an AI tool and doesn't intend to, and she trusts the co-op and the union far more than any company. In the mild scenarios she is calm or mildly uneasy, worried mainly that the landowners might rent to a robot contractor. With two years of warning she expects to lose the lease and sell her flock, and she is frightened and angry. With five or ten years she can line the change up with her own retirement, so her worry moves to her neighbour and her son.
biggestWorry: AGI arriving within two years, because she would lose her tenancy before she's ready to stop farming and could do nothing about it on her own.
whatWouldHelp: A law giving tenant farmers first refusal and a fair notice period, and a pension top-up for people who have farmed since they were sixteen.
